# PREFATORY NOTE TO GENESIS.

WHEN the task of preparing the larger Cambridge edition of the Septuagint <note>The Septuagint, often abbreviated as LXX, is the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to have been translated by seventy-two Jewish scholars.</note> was entrusted to the present editors by the Syndics of the University Press in 1895, it was settled that the first volume should contain the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament: Genesis through Ruth.</note> (Genesis to Ruth). As the collection and arrangement of material have occupied a much longer time than was anticipated, it has been decided to publish the first volume in four parts—containing (1) Genesis, (2) Exodus and Leviticus, (3) Numbers and Deuteronomy, and (4) Joshua, Judges and Ruth—in order to place the information we have collected at the disposal of scholars as soon as possible. We are not yet able to present in final form our preface to the Octateuch, and must here confine ourselves to lists of the symbols and abbreviations used, with a short explanation of the methods adopted in our critical notes.

The object of our work is to present as clearly and fully as is possible within reasonable limits of space the evidence available for the reconstruction of the text or texts of the Septuagint. At an early stage of the undertaking it was decided that it would be premature to attempt to provide a reconstructed or “true” text in this edition; and that the text of the Vatican Manuscript <note>A 4th-century Greek manuscript, one of the oldest and most complete survivors of the Bible.</note> should be followed wherever extant, its gaps being supplied from the Alexandrian or another uncial <note>A style of writing using large, rounded capital letters, typical of Greek manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries.</note> manuscript. The text of Dr Swete’s manual edition has therefore been reprinted with but few alterations. The punctuation has been revised, and a few departures from the text of the principal manuscript have been made in cases where its readings are quite indefensible. Daggers († †) have been used to indicate all such departures from the manuscript which are not merely corrections of itacisms <note>Spelling variations caused by different Greek vowels coming to be pronounced the same way, like 'ee' and 'ih'.</note>, misspellings, or trivial errors of a similar kind.

The symbol placed at the top of the outer margin on each page is that of the manuscript which supplies the text. A list of the manuscripts and versions quoted in the notes is given in a line between the first and second sets of notes. Where an authority is extant for part of a page only, its symbol is placed in brackets.

1. The notes immediately below the text contain the itacisms and small errors of the principal manuscript, as well as of the other uncial manuscripts quoted in the manual edition, but not of the remaining uncials, nor of any cursive <note>A later, flowing style of Greek handwriting, similar to modern script.</note> manuscripts.¹ After the first 20 chapters of Genesis were in type, we decided from this point onwards to include in these notes also all readings of the principal manuscript which are not adopted in the text, and notes on corrections in this manuscript by the first or by later scribes. Its substantial variants are repeated in the main notes only where they are supported by other authorities or are important for the interpretation of the whole evidence.

2. In the main body of notes we have endeavoured to give the substantial variants found in (*a*) all the extant uncial manuscripts and the 30 cursive manuscripts selected by us as representative, (*b*) the chief ancient versions made from the Septuagint, (*c*) the writings of Philo, Josephus, and the most important of the early Christian writers. With a view to

---

¹ We are anxious to reproduce all the information contained in the notes of the manual edition, but do not think it well, in view of the large number of authorities quoted, to cumber our notes with the small details of other manuscripts than those used by Dr Swete.

# PREFATORY NOTE

For the sake of completeness, moreover, variants which are quoted by Holmes and Parsons <note>Robert Holmes and James Parsons edited a famous five-volume edition of the Septuagint (1798–1827) which this text references.</note> from any of their manuscripts, but are not found in any of the manuscripts selected by us, are given between angular brackets ⟨ ⟩ on the authority of their edition, the manuscripts so quoted being denoted by Holmes’s numbers.

The number of authorities quoted has made it desirable to exclude impossible forms and constructions, and minutiae <note>Small or trivial details.</note> devoid of special interest or value: but it has not been possible to follow rigid rules with absolute consistency. In recording possible variants, which may be only itacistic <note>A common scribal error in Greek where different vowels or diphthongs that sounded alike—such as 'i', 'ei', and 'oi'—were swapped.</note> blunders, we have been to some extent guided by the character of the manuscript which contains them. Where a reading is found in only one manuscript, its spelling is reproduced. Where two or more manuscripts have the same reading but show unimportant differences in spelling, all are credited with the forms of words such as are usually followed in the text. But in the case of proper names we have endeavoured to give all variations of spelling with the exception of such itacisms as the interchange of ι <note>iota</note> and ει <note>epsilon-iota</note>, and (in some cases) of ε <note>epsilon</note> and αι <note>alpha-iota</note>.

In the arrangement of the notes the order of the text has of course been followed; and variants on longer portions of the text precede those on shorter portions beginning with the same word. In each set of variants words prefixed to those of the text are given first (introduced by “pr” <note>Latin: *praemittit*, meaning 'prefixes'.</note>), then alternative words, and then words added after those of the text (introduced by +). Except in the case where words are prefixed or added, we have tried to avoid quoting the same authority twice in the same set of variants—unless one of the points in question is a mere detail of spelling. But we have not always been able to carry out this rule consistently. To discover the exact reading of any manuscript it is important that readers should look through the whole list of variants on the particular word or phrase in question.

When an addition or alternative reading of some length is supported by several authorities, the commonest form of the reading is given first, followed by the symbols of all the authorities which yield it general support: then the detailed variations of each authority from that type are added in double brackets ⟦ ⟧. This method, besides saving a great deal of space, seems to show clearly at a glance what authorities really support many of the more important variants. In the case of these and other readings, where one authority differs in a single detail from the common type shown by the authorities which otherwise support the same reading, the difference has been recorded in ordinary brackets ( ) immediately after the symbol of that authority. Where several agree in one divergence, it has been recorded in similar brackets after the list of symbols.

When the reading of the text has the support of comparatively few manuscripts, the positive evidence has been given immediately after the word or phrase quoted from the text and to the left of the square bracket. In such cases the symbols of those cursives <note>Manuscripts written in a running, connected script, common from the 9th century onwards.</note> which support the commonest variant are not separately enumerated, except where there has been correction by later hands, but are included under “rell” <note>Latin: *reliqui*, meaning 'the rest'.</note> (or “omn” <note>Latin: *omnes*, meaning 'all'.</note> if all the cursives are agreed). But the symbols of all authorities other than Greek cursives are in these cases given in full. If any are omitted it is because their evidence is not decisive for or against the particular variant.

Our treatment of the several ancient versions has varied according to the character of each. The evidence of the Old Latin has been given with special fullness, not only because of its intrinsic importance, but also because of its relation to the Scripture citations of the Latin Fathers. The Syro-hexaplar <note>A 7th-century Syriac translation of the Greek Septuagint as revised by Origen.</note> is fully quoted for a different reason, viz. its extreme literalness, and the certainty with which it can be retranslated into Greek. The Armenian has the same quality though in a less degree: and the character of the

### TO GENESIS

->b 2<-

Palestinian Aramaic <note>A dialect of Aramaic used in the Holy Land during the early centuries of the Common Era.</note>, where it is extant, is similar. The Ethiopic <note>The ancient liturgical language of Ethiopia, also known as Ge’ez.</note> is too free to be quoted without great caution, and from the middle of Genesis onward the use of its evidence has been confined almost entirely to the cases where it agrees with some other authority or with the Hebrew original: much space has thus been saved without serious detriment<sup>1</sup>. The Egyptian versions are on the whole accurate translations, though they do not follow the Greek so slavishly as the Syro-hexaplar <note>A 7th-century Syriac translation of the Greek Old Testament as it appeared in Origen’s "Hexapla," a massive multi-columned scholarly edition.</note>, and the Sahidic <note>A dialect of the Coptic language used in Upper/Southern Egypt.</note> sometimes betrays a tendency to paraphrase. The evidence for some unimportant variants in the Coptic versions is very uncertain, for example as regards the copula <note>A word, such as "and," that links parts of a sentence.</note> before verbs (particularly in narrative), the article, and pronouns affixed to nouns and verbs. In all these cases the evidence of the version has been neglected unless it is supported by other authority<sup>2</sup>. Where the weak article is used in Coptic, the version has not been cited for or against the presence of the article in Greek<sup>3</sup>.

The evidence of the versions has been quoted in Latin wherever their variants are unsupported by Greek authorities. The original languages are quoted only in a few instances where it seems necessary to emphasize some point which is in itself doubtful or which cannot be clearly expressed in Latin. The forms of proper names found in the Latin and Egyptian versions have usually been given in full, and so too the Armenian forms of all but those that frequently occur<sup>4</sup>. The forms of proper names found in the Syro-hexaplar have in the great majority of instances been neglected, as agreeing with those found in the Peshitta <note>The "simple" or standard Syriac translation of the Bible.</note> and evidently derived from that source: but wherever they deviate from the Peshitta form they have been given in the Syriac character, since there is no sufficiently trustworthy witness to their vocalisation. In the Ethiopic version the proper names are so constantly distorted and corrupt, that it has seemed best to neglect altogether its evidence on this head.

The redaction of patristic evidence <note>Quotations of the Bible found in the writings of the early "Church Fathers."</note> has proved in some ways the most difficult and least satisfactory part of our work. To the well-known difficulties due to the unsatisfactory state of the text of most editions of the Fathers, and to the habit shewn by many writers of quoting inexactly from memory, is added that which arises from the reaction of New Testament quotations of certain passages, which were more familiar to the writers in this form than in the actual Greek of the Septuagint. There are many instances too of "conflate" quotations, where elements derived from different passages of the Old Testament have been interwoven. The fractions which indicate the proportion of support that a variant receives from a Father as compared with the total number of his quotations of the passage must be regarded as only roughly approximate. They take account only of those passages which we have decided to treat as definite quotations with respect to the particular variants to which they are attached. It is not always easy to decide whether the repetition of a verse, or part of it, in the near neighbourhood of a quotation should be treated as a separate attestation of the words. The improved texts of the Berlin and Vienna editions have been used wherever available<sup>5</sup>: but in most other cases we have had

<header>PREFATORY NOTE</header>

to depend on unsatisfactory texts. This is shown only too clearly by the frequency with which two or more variants receive about equal support from the same writer. And it must be added that even when satisfactory editions of all the Church Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians whose writings are used to track how the biblical text changed over time.</note> are available, it will still be difficult to estimate the value of their evidence without considering each quotation with special reference to its context in the works of the writer who makes it.

Of evidence derived from the writings of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Jewish historian whose works provide insight into 1st-century biblical interpretation.</note> we have been able to make little use: his relation to the text of the Septuagint <term>LXX: The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</term>—so far as he used it at all—is quite different in kind from that of the other writers whose quotations we have given. The questions of the sources from which he derived his own account of facts recorded in the Old Testament, and of his method in dealing with his materials, are such as lie outside the scope of our undertaking.

3. Our third set of notes contains the hexaplaric <term>Material relating to the *Hexapla*, a massive six-columned scholarly edition of the Old Testament created by Origen in the 3rd century to compare different Greek and Hebrew versions.</term> matter found in the margins of those manuscripts which we quote continuously, and of the Syro-hexaplar version. We did not think it our duty to include in our selection all manuscripts with marginal hexaplaric matter, or to collect such matter from other sources, for the result would only have been the reprinting of the greater part of Field’s *Hexapla* <note>A definitive 1875 collection of these fragments by Frederick Field.</note>. But when a manuscript was chosen for its own text, it seemed desirable to give the whole of its evidence. We have thus added a certain amount of new matter not given by Field, but none of this is of great importance.

Our task has been greatly lightened by the generous contributions of many friends and fellow-workers, who have helped us with the collation <term>The process of comparing different manuscripts to identify variations.</term> and photographing of manuscripts, and with the collection of patristic quotations. But we must postpone detailed acknowledgement till the publication of the first volume as a whole.

There is however no need to delay the acknowledgement of our debt to those whose work is done. The obvious defects of the great Oxford edition of the Septuagint by Holmes and Parsons <note>An influential edition published between 1798 and 1827.</note>, when judged by critical standards of a later age, have unfortunately done much to obscure its enormous value, especially in the volume which contains the Pentateuch <term>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</term>. The amount and completeness of the information from Greek manuscripts which this edition supplies is the more surprising the more the subject is studied. To have collected the readings of practically all the manuscripts of the Septuagint which were then in Europe, during the stormy years at the end of the 18th and beginning of the 19th century, was a very remarkable feat. Without this pioneer work our task would have been almost impossible, and it is only just to recognize the extent of our debt to the Oxford editors.

Among the Septuagint scholars of the 19th century the name of Lagarde <note>Paul de Lagarde (1827–1891), a brilliant but notoriously difficult German scholar of oriental languages and the Bible.</note> stands first. His contributions to the subject are too well known to need special mention here. But it would be impossible to publish our work without declaring our indebtedness to them. In April 1868 he wrote “With my edition of Genesis, however, I shall endeavor to train young men who may be able to assist me in preparing an edition of the entire Greek Old Testament; for I am entirely unable to sustain such a great labor alone” <note>original Latin: "Mea autem Genesis editione conabor uti ad instituendos iuuenes, qui integri ueteris testamenti graeci editionem parantem me possint adiuuare: nam solus tantum laborem sustinere omnino nequeo."</note>. He alone, if any one, could have “sustained the labour”—not only of the preliminary task which has been entrusted to us, but also of its more important sequel—the reconstruction of the pre-hexaplaric text of the Septuagint, so far as that is now possible. We gladly testify to what we have learned from his edition of *Genesis*, as well as from his other writings.

Once more, it is always a pleasure to Cambridge men to have an opportunity of recording their obligations to Dr Hort <note>Fenton John Anthony Hort (1828–1892), a seminal figure in New Testament and Septuagint textual criticism at Cambridge.</note>. It is altogether characteristic of him that though his name is nowhere publicly connected with Septuagint studies the determination of the scope of this edition was entirely his work. In his memorandum on the extent and value of extant authorities for the text of the Septuagint the lines are laid down which have been

His hints on the best method of describing manuscripts, and of collecting the evidence of patristic citations <note>References to the Bible found in the writings of the early Church Fathers.</note>, have guided the labors of those who have helped us, as well as our own. And all his pupils would say of him, as Gregory said of Origen, that much as they learned from his words they learned more from his example—he encouraged them more by his deeds than by what he said <note>original: παρεκάλει πλέον τοῖς ἔργοις ἢ οἷς ἔλεγεν</note>.

To all those connected with the University Press who have been employed on the printing of our work we would express our sincere thanks for the accuracy and skill with which they have carried out their task.

<meta>This page provides a key to the symbols and abbreviations used in the critical apparatus—the detailed notes at the bottom of the main text that show differences between various manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament.</meta>

# ABBREVIATIONS.

**around** <note>original: "circ = circiter"</note> = approximately.
**manuscript** <note>original: "cod = codex"</note> = i.e. one manuscript.
**only manuscript** <note>original: "cod-unic = codex unicus"</note> = the only surviving manuscript.
**manuscripts** <note>original: "codd = codices"</note> = i.e. two or more manuscripts.
**all manuscripts** <note>original: "codd-omn = codices omnes"</note> = all the surviving manuscripts.
**in the edition** <note>original: "ed = in editione"</note> = i.e. according to the text of the printed edition used.
**from a correction** <note>original: "ex corr = ex correctura"</note>.
**outside the lines** <note>original: "ext lin = extra lineas"</note> = i.e. projecting beyond the beginning or end of a line.
**included** <note>original: "incl = inclusit or incluserunt"</note>.
**wrote in** <note>original: "inscr = inscripsit or inscripserunt"</note>.
**between the lines** <note>original: "int lin = intra lineas"</note> = i.e. above or below the line.
**in the margin** <note>original: "mg = in margine"</note>.
**omits** <note>original: "om = omittit or omuntunt"</note>.
**all** <note>original: "omn = omnes"</note> = i.e. all the selected cursive <note>a style of Greek handwriting with joined letters</note> manuscripts.
**prefixes** <note>original: "pr = praemittit or praemittunt"</note> = places before.
**erased** <note>original: "ras = rasum or rasura"</note>. **Erased (1)**, **erased (2)** mean one letter erased, two letters erased, and so on.

# OTHER SIGNS.

**:** is used to separate variations on the same word or phrase.
**|** is used to separate variations on one word or phrase from those on another.
**]** separates the word or phrase in the text from the variations on it. *Note:* The mention of the word or phrase in the text is omitted where there is only one variation, and it is obvious to what word or phrase it belongs. Where positive evidence is quoted (see above, page ii) it is given between the word or phrase and the square bracket.
**[ ]** Words or parts of words which cannot be clearly read are enclosed in square brackets.
**( )** after a symbol contain a peculiarity of spelling or wording found only in that authority. Where however symbols are included within the brackets the peculiarity is found in all the authorities so denoted.
**(?)**, which indicates doubt, usually refers only to the letter immediately preceding.
**( )** containing a number (1) when prefixed to a word taken from the text indicate the verse to which it belongs, (2) after "**erased**" <note>original: "ras"</note> indicate the number of letters erased.
**[[ ]]** See above, page ii.
**< >** enclose all information which is given on the authority of Holmes and Parsons <note>scholars who produced a famous 18th-century edition of the Septuagint</note>.
**+** introduces an addition which comes after the words quoted from the text.
**-** In any list of cursive manuscripts, a-d = abcd, k-n = klmn, and so on.

<column-break/>

**recent hand** <note>original: "rec man = recenti manu"</note> = written by a later scribe.
**rewritten** <note>original: "rescr = rescripsit"</note>.
**the rest** <note>original: "rell = reliqui"</note> = i.e. the rest of the selected cursive manuscripts.
**or** <note>original: "s. = siue"</note>.
**without name** <note>original: "sine nom = sine nomine s. nominibus"</note> = i.e. with the omission of the signs for the Greek translators Aquila, Symmachus, etc.
**wrote at the end** <note>original: "subscr = subscripsit or subscripserunt"</note>.
**over an erasure** <note>original: "sup ras = supra rasuram"</note>.
**written above** <note>original: "suprascr = suprascriptit"</note>.
**in the text** <note>original: "txt = in textu"</note>.
**apparently** <note>original: "uid = ut uidetur"</note>.
**Aquila** <note>original: "α' = 'Ακύλας"</note>. <note>Aquila of Sinope was a 2nd-century translator known for his literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>
**the Hebrew** <note>original: "εβρ = ὁ ἑβραῖος"</note>.
**Theodotion** <note>original: "θ' = Θεοδοτίων"</note>. <note>A 2nd-century translator whose work often revised earlier Greek versions.</note>
**the others** <note>original: "οι λ = οἱ λοιποί"</note> = i.e. the other translators.
**Symmachus** <note>original: "σ' = Σύμμαχος"</note>. <note>An late 2nd-century translator who aimed for more idiomatic Greek than Aquila.</note>
**the Samaritan** <note>original: "σαμ. = τὸ σαμαρειτικόν"</note>. <note>Referring to the Samaritan Pentateuch.</note>

**——** between two words taken from the text indicates that the intervening words are included.
**...** between two words taken from the text indicates that the intervening words are not included in those for which the variants form an equivalent.
**...** at the end of an incomplete word or phrase indicates that the completion is wanting or cannot be read.
**begins** <note>original: "§ = incipit"</note>.
**ends** <note>original: "¶ = explicit"</note>.
**† †** are placed before and after words in the text in respect of which the reading of the principal manuscript has been departed from.
**※** is the hexaplaric asterisk <note>a sign used by the scholar Origen to mark words in the Greek text that were present in the Hebrew but missing in the original Septuagint</note>.
**÷** is the hexaplaric obelus <note>a sign used to mark words in the Greek text that were not present in the Hebrew</note>. Varying forms of this (⸓ ~) are only noted for the manuscript S.
**˅** is the hexaplaric metobelus <note>a sign marking the end of a passage labeled with an asterisk or obelus</note>.
**1st, 2nd, etc.** <note>original: "1°, 2°, &c."</note> indicate the first, second, etc. time the word or phrase occurs in the verse.
A fraction after the name of an authority shows by the denominator the number of times that the words in question are quoted by that authority, and by the numerator the number of times that it supports the particular variation. Thus, for example, **Cyr 2/3-ed 1/4-cod 1/1** means that out of four quotations of the word in Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Bishop</note>, two have the particular variation according to all the evidence known to us; in the third quotation the edited <note>printed</note> text of Cyril has it, but a manuscript or manuscripts differ; while in the fourth case only one manuscript is known to have the variation, which is not found in the edited text of the Church Father.

# GENESIS OF THE WORLD

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
§ IN THE BEGINNING God made the heaven and the earth. ²But the earth was invisible and unformed, <margin>A $\mathfrak{U}_2$</margin> <note>These symbols refer to specific ancient manuscripts: A is the Codex Alexandrinus (5th century) and $\mathfrak{U}_2$ is a papyrus fragment.</note>
<margin>3</margin> and darkness was over the abyss; and the spirit of God was moving over the water. ³And
<margin>4</margin> God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light. ⁴And God saw the light, that it was good; and God
<margin>5</margin> divided between the light and between the darkness. ⁵And God called
the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one
<margin>6</margin> day. ¶ ⁶And God said, “Let there be a firmament <note>The "firmament" (Greek: steréoma) refers to a solid dome or expanse that ancient people believed separated the waters of the heavens from the waters of the earth.</note> in the midst of the water, and let it be dividing <margin>$\mathfrak{U}_2$</margin>
<margin>7</margin> between water and water”; and it was so. ⁷And God made the firmament; and God
divided between the water which was under the firmament, and between the water
<margin>8</margin> which was above the firmament. ⁸And God called the firmament Heaven; and God saw that it was
<margin>9</margin> good. And there was evening and there was morning, a second day. ⁹And God said, “Let the
water under the heaven be gathered together into one gathering, and let the dry land appear”; and it was
so. And the water under the heaven was gathered into their gatherings, and the dry land appeared.
<margin>10</margin> ¹⁰And God called the dry land Earth, and the collections of waters He called Seas;
<margin>11</margin> and God saw that it was good. ¹¹And God said, “Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass, sowing

# GENESIS II 23

14 [The name of the] second [river] is Gihon; this is the one circling all the land of Ethiopia. **14** And the third river is the Tigris; 
15 this is the one flowing opposite the Assyrians. And the fourth river, this is the Euphrates. **15** And 
the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise, to work 
16 it and to guard it. **16** And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: "From every tree 
17 in the paradise you may freely eat; **17** but from the tree of knowing good and evil, you 
18 shall not eat from it; for on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die." **18** And 
the Lord God said: "It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper corresponding to him." **19** And 
God still formed from the earth all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the sky, and 
he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and whatever Adam called 
20 a living soul, that was its name. **20** And Adam gave names to all the cattle and to all the 
birds of the sky and to all the beasts of the field; but for Adam there was not found a helper like 
21 him. **21** And God cast a deep sleep <note>The Greek word *ekstasis* implies a trance or a divinely induced deep slumber.</note> upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his 
22 ribs and filled up the flesh in its place. **22** And the Lord God built the rib, 
23 which he took from Adam, into a woman; and he brought her to Adam. **23** And Adam 
said: "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman..."

->**Textual variations in the primary manuscripts:**
17 "you shall eat"] spelled as "to eat" in Manuscripts A and E | "you shall eat" (different Greek verb form) in A. 
20 "all the cattle"] Manuscript E uses a feminine form.
22 "built"] variant spelling in the original hand of Manuscript E. 
23 "bone"] omitted by Manuscript A.<-

->**List of manuscript witnesses cited below:**
Manuscripts E, M, a, b, d, j, l, r, s, t, v, y, c, d, and Codices A, B, E, P.<-

**14** "the" is omitted by manuscript *e* | "Tigris"] preceded by "the" in 2 out of 3 manuscripts of Philo | "Tigris" is spelled differently in several manuscripts | "this" replaced by "he" in Manuscript M | "flowing"] preceded by "the river" in E; "preceding" in M and y | "Assyrians"] spelled with one 's' in some copies; "Assyria" in Codex A and Philo's Armenian version | "and the [river]" replaced by "and the" in some versions | "this" (the second instance) is omitted in several manuscripts; Manuscript *g* adds "is the great one" | "Euphrates"] preceded by "the" in some; spelled "Euphrates" in others; some manuscripts add "this is the great river"; the Latin Codex C adds "the great river."

**15** "Lord" is omitted by manuscript 37 | "formed"] replaced by "made" in several manuscripts | "him" (the first instance) is omitted in some copies | "paradise"] several manuscripts add "of luxury" <note>This is the Greek way of translating "Eden," which sounds like the word for pleasure/luxury.</note> | "him" (the second instance) is omitted by one version of Theodoret | "guard"] several manuscripts add "him" (as in, "guarding him").

**16** "Lord" is omitted by some | "tree"] preceded by "the" in one manuscript | "freely" is omitted in some manuscripts of Philo and Chrysostom | "you may eat"] variant verb forms "you shall eat" or "to eat."

**17** "the tree"] preceded by "the fruit" in one version | "knowing... evil"] "knowing the known things of good and evil" in one version | "and"] replaced by "or" in some Philo manuscripts | "you shall not eat"] variant spellings and verb forms | "from it" (first instance)] "out of it" in some; omitted in Codex A; one manuscript adds "nor shall you touch it, lest you die" | "on whatever day"] variant grammar in several manuscripts | "you eat"] many variants including "you shall eat," "you might eat," or "you have eaten" | "from it" (second instance)] "from the tree" in Chrysostom; omitted by others | "by death you shall die"] "you shall die" (singular) in one; "he shall die" in others.

**18** "Lord" is omitted by some | "the man"] omitted by manuscript 31 | "let us make"] "I will make" in some Philo manuscripts | "him"] "them" or "his" in a few versions.

**19** "formed"] "called" in one manuscript | "God still"] some add "Lord"; others omit "still" | "God"] adds "the man" in one copy | "from the earth"] omitted by Codex A | "every" (first instance)] preceded by "and" | "birds... sky"] "cattle" in one version of Chrysostom | "brought"] "led" | "to see what..."] omitted in some versions | "whatever"] variant forms of "if" or "what" | "it"] variant "them" or omitted | "Adam" (second instance)] preceded by "the"; omitted by some; one version adds "of them" | "living soul"] preceded by "into a" in some | "that"] "was" added in one version | "its name"] "the name"; "their name"; "to them."

**20** "and" (first instance)] omitted in one | "Adam" (first instance)] preceded by "the"; omitted in E | "name"] plural "names" in E | "all... and" (second instance)] omitted in some | "cattle"] variant word order | "birds... field"] "beasts" omitted in E; "field" replaced by "earth" in many versions | "but"] the Greek *te* in A is replaced by *de* in most other versions | "was not found"] "there was not" | "helper"] moved in word order | "like him"] one version adds "corresponding to him."

**21** "God"] many manuscripts add "Lord" | "one of the ribs"] the Latin Codex B reads "a rib from the sides" | "filled up"] variant Greek verbs for "closed up" or "replaced" | "its"] "their" in one manuscript.

**22** "Lord God"] "God" or "Lord" omitted in some | "from Adam"] omitted in one | "and he brought... Adam"] omitted in one.

**23** "Adam"] preceded by "to him" | "now"] "therefore"; "it was"; or "is" in Latin versions; omitted by some | "and flesh of my flesh"] omitted in one version | "flesh" (second instance)] plural "fleshes" in one.

->**Philological Notes from Ancient Translators:**
**14** "opposite"] Aquila and Symmachus translate this as "from the east."
**17** "on whatever day you eat"] Aquila: "that in the day of your eating"; Symmachus: "for on the day." | "by death you shall die"] The "Others" (anonymous Greek versions): "you shall be mortal."
**18** "alone"] Aquila and others: "solitary"; Symmachus: "solitary." | "corresponding to him"] Aquila: "as if opposite him"; Symmachus: "directly facing him."
**19** "beasts"] Symmachus: "living creatures."
**20** "beasts"] Aquila and Symmachus: "living creatures." | "like him"] Symmachus: "directly facing him"; Aquila: "directly facing him."
**21** "deep sleep"] Aquila: "deep slumber"; Symmachus: "torpor" or "numbness." | "filled up"] Aquila: "closed up"; Symmachus: "shut together."
**23** "this now"] Symmachus and Theodotion: "this once." | "Woman... because she was taken from man"] A note on the Hebrew: "*Issa* [woman] is the taking, or the 'man-ess'; she shall be called 'man-ess' because she was taken from man."<-

**Alternative Greek Translations (Hexapla):**
<note>This section compares the standard Septuagint with other ancient Greek versions: Aquila (α'), Symmachus (σ'), and Theodotion (θ').</note>

**Verse 7:** "his turning and you shall rule over him" — Aquila: "if you do well, you will be accepted, but if you do not do well, sin lies at the door, and its impulse is toward you, but you shall have mastery over it." | Symmachus: "if you do well... sin lies at the door..." [similar to Aquila].
**8** "Let us go out into the field" — This phrase seems to have been taken from an apocryphal source by Symmachus; it is also in the Samaritan Pentateuch, but it is not written in the Hebrew or in the version of Aquila.
**12** "and it shall no longer yield" — Symmachus: "it will no longer." | "groaning and trembling" — Symmachus: "uprooted and unstable." : the Hebrew and the Syrian: "shaking and unstable."
**13** "my punishment" — Aquila: "my lawlessness."
**14** "if you cast me out" — Aquila: "behold, you have cast me out."
**15** "sevenfold vengeance" — Aquila: *seven times shall he be vindicated*. Symmachus: *seven times shall he give vengeance*. Theodotion: *he shall vindicate through the week*. A Syrian note: "He whom he begot in the seventh generation will give vengeance." | "to kill" — Aquila: "to strike"; Symmachus: "to beat."
**16** "Nod" — "uprooted, commotion, shaking" : Symmachus: "uprooted, of commotion, or shaking" : "commotion" : Symmachus: *rebellious (?)* : Theodotion: *fluctuating*.

<meta>This page transitions from the narrative of Noah’s post-flood life and his vineyard to the formal genealogical record of his descendants. This page concludes the story of Noah with his death and begins the "Table of Nations," identifying the ancestors of various ethnic and linguistic groups known to the ancient world.</meta>

# GENESIS X 10

$^{28}$ And Noah lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years. $^{29}$ And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

---

**X 1** Now these are the generations of the sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth; and sons were born to them after the flood. ¶
**2** The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan and Elisa <margin>wd2</margin> and Thobel and Mosoch and Thiras.
**3** And the sons of Gomer: Aschanaz and Riphath and Thergama.
**4** And the sons of Javan: Elisa and Tharsis, the Kittim <note>The Greek "Kētioi" refers to the people of Cyprus or the coastlands</note>, and the Rhodians.
**5** From these the islands of the nations were set apart in their lands; each according to their language in their tribes and in their nations.
**6** And the sons of Ham: Chous <note>Traditionally identified with Cush/Ethiopia</note> and Mestrain <note>Traditionally identified with Egypt</note>, Phoud and Canaan.
**7** And the sons of Chous: Saba and Euila and Sabatha and Regchama and Sabakatha. And the sons of Regchama: Saba and Dadan.
**8** And Chous fathered Nebrod <note>Known in other translations as Nimrod</note>; he began to be a giant upon the earth.
**9** He was a giant hunter before the Lord God; because of this they shall say, "Like Nebrod, a giant hunter before the Lord."
**10** And the beginning [of his kingdom] was...

# GENESIS

...of the East. ³¹ These are the sons of *Shem* <note>The manuscript A (Codex Alexandrinus) reads "Sheth" here instead of "Shem"</note> in their tribes, according to their languages, in their lands and in their nations. ³² These are the tribes of the sons of Noah according to their generations, according to their nations; from these the islands of the nations were scattered over the earth after the flood <note>original: "kataklysmos," the source of the English word "cataclysm"</note>.

¹ And all the earth was of one lip <note>A literal translation of the Greek "cheilos," meaning they spoke a single language</note>, and there was one voice for all. ² And it happened that as they moved from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar <note>original: "Sennaar"</note> and settled there. ³ And a man said to his neighbor, "Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire." And the brick served them as stone, and bitumen <note>original: "asphaltos"</note> served them as mortar. ⁴ And they said, "Come, let us build for ourselves a city and a tower, whose top shall reach to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves before we are scattered over the face of all the earth." ⁵ And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built. ⁶ And the Lord said, "Behold, they are one race and one lip for all; and they have begun to do this, and now nothing will fail from them <note>The sense is that nothing they propose will be impossible for them</note>, whatever they may undertake to do. ⁷ Come, let us go down and there confuse <note>original: "syncheōmen," meaning to pour together or mingle</note> their language, so that they may not understand each other's voice." ⁸ And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city and the tower. ⁹ Because of this, its name was called Confusion <note>original: "Synchysis." In Hebrew, this is "Babel," which the Greek translators rendered by its meaning, "Confusion"</note>, because there...

# GENESIS XII 9
### Page 29

**XII** $^1$ § $^1$ And the Lord said to Abram: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from the house of your father, into the land that I will show you. $^2$ And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless <margin>§ d₂</margin> you and magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. $^3$ And I will bless those who bless you, and those who curse you I will curse, and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” $^4$ And Abram went just as the Lord had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. Now Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran. $^5$ And Abram took his wife Sara and Lot, the son of his brother, and all their possessions which they had acquired, and every soul <note>original: "psuchēn," referring to people or servants</note> they had acquired in Haran, and they went out to go into the land of Canaan; and they came into the land of Canaan. $^6$ And Abram traveled through the length of it as far as the place of Shechem, to the high oak <note>This is the famous "Oak of Moreh"; the Greek Septuagint translates it as "high oak."</note>; and the Canaanites then inhabited the land. $^7$ And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him: “To your offspring I will give this land.” And Abram built an altar there to the Lord who had appeared to him. ¶ $^8$ And he departed from there to the mountain east of Bethel, and he pitched <margin>¶ d₂</margin> his tent there with Bethel toward the sea <note>In biblical geography, "toward the sea" usually means West, toward the Mediterranean.</note> and Ai toward the east; and he built an altar there to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord. $^9$ And Abram set out and, journeying on, he camped in the desert.

<meta>This page continues the biblical narrative of Abram (later Abraham) in the land of Canaan. Following the dispute between his herdsmen and those of his nephew Lot, the two have agreed to part ways. Lot has chosen the fertile Jordan valley, moving toward Sodom, while Abram remains in the highlands. This page records God’s renewed promise to Abram and the beginning of a regional conflict between several ancient kings.</meta>

### Critical Notes on Manuscript Variants
<note>This section compares different ancient copies of the Bible, such as the Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), and various early translations (Ethiopic, Armenian, etc.) to show how the text varied between communities.</note>

**Verse 7:** [The word "calf"] is omitted in manuscripts A, B, C, and E, and in the Armenian and Latin versions. | [calf] is placed after the word "tender" in manuscript 31. | [and good] is omitted in the Armenian version and some Greek manuscripts. | [gave] is written as [has given] in manuscript 78. | [to the servant] is written as [to his servants] in the Ethiopic version. | [he hastened] is written as [they hastened] in the Ethiopic.

**Verse 8:** [took] is preceded by [and] in some copies. | [milk] includes [unleavened bread] in some Palestinian versions. | [and he ate] occurs in manuscripts A and Y, but the rest of the manuscripts use slightly different forms of the verb. | [by them... tree] is written as [under the tree and he was serving them] in some versions.

**Verse 9:** [he said] is written as [they said] in several manuscripts. | [answering] is omitted in some Syriac and Palestinian versions.

**Verse 10:** [And he said] is omitted in manuscript D. | [at this time] is omitted in some early fragments. | [next season] is written as [next year] in some Coptic manuscripts. | [Sarah your wife] is shortened by omitting [the wife] in some versions. | [behind him] is omitted in the writings of the church father Chrysostom.

**Verse 11:** [elderly] is omitted in some manuscripts. | [advanced] is preceded by the word [the]. | [manner of women]—the entire phrase is omitted in manuscript d₂. | [had ceased] uses a slightly different Greek spelling across various manuscripts.

**Verse 12:** [Sarah laughed] is written as [And she laughed] in some copies. | [within herself] is written as [to herself] or [by herself] in others. | [This... until now] is translated in the Armenian version as [that which has not yet been done to me now shall be]. | [elderly] is replaced with [advanced in days] in some Coptic fragments.

**Verse 13:** [Lord] is preceded by [God] in some manuscripts. | [Why] is written as [What] in some major codices. | [within herself] is omitted in some early citations.

**Verse 14:** [Is impossible] is written as [Will be impossible] in some versions. | [with God]—some versions use [with the Lord]. | [word] is preceded by [any] or [every] in many copies. | [at this time] is preceded by [behold I] in some versions.

**Verse 15:** [Sarah] is preceded by [the] in several Greek copies. | [denied] is followed by [that] in the Armenian version. | [said] is followed by [to her] in several manuscripts.

**Verse 16:** [rose up... looked] is translated as [and they went from there and he looked up] in Coptic. | [men] is preceded by [three] in some manuscripts, while others say [two]. | [Abraham]—some versions omit [with them].

**Verse 17:** [The Lord said] is written as [The Lord said to Abraham, saying to him] in some Coptic copies. | [Hide from]—some versions use [Be hidden from]. | [what I am doing] is written as [what I am about to do] in some citations.

**Verse 18:** [becoming] is written as [having become] in some Greek manuscripts. | [and numerous] is written as [and strong] in others.

# GENESIS XXI 21

<margin>11</margin> Isaac. ¹¹But the matter appeared very harsh before Abraham regarding his son Ishmael. 
<margin>12</margin> ¹²But God said to Abraham: "Let the matter not be harsh before you regarding the child and regarding the maidservant; in all things that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice; for in Isaac your seed shall be called <note>original: κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα — meaning your descendants will be named through Isaac’s line</note>. 
<margin>13</margin> ¹³And the son of this maidservant, I will make him into a great nation, because he is your seed." 
<margin>14</margin> ¹⁴And Abraham rose early in the morning, and took bread and a skin of water and gave them to Hagar, and placed them upon her shoulder along with the child, and sent her away. And having departed, she wandered in the wilderness near the Well of the Oath <note>original: φρέαρ τοῦ ὅρκου (Phrear tou horkou), the Greek translation of the Hebrew 'Beersheba'</note>. 
<margin>15</margin> ¹⁵And the water failed from the skin, and she cast the child beneath a fir tree <note>original: ἐλάτης (elates) — while often 'fir' or 'pine,' in this desert context it refers to a scrubby bush or tree providing meager shade</note>. 
<margin>16</margin> ¹⁶And having gone away, she sat down opposite him at a distance, about a bowshot away; for she said, "Let me not see the death of my child." And she sat opposite him from a distance; and the child cried out and wept. 
<margin>17</margin> ¹⁷And God heard the voice of the child from the place where he was, and an angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What is it, Hagar? Do not fear; for God has heard the voice of your child from the place where he is. 
<margin>18 19</margin> ¹⁸Rise and take the child, and hold him by your hand; for I will make him into a great nation." ¹⁹And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water; and she went and filled the skin with water and gave the child to drink. 
<margin>20</margin> ²⁰And God was with the child, and he grew; and he dwelt in the wilderness; and he became an archer. 
<margin>21</margin> ²¹And he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran. <margin>¶</margin> And his mother took for him a wife from the land of Egypt.

# XXI 22 GENESIS

<margin>A</margin> ²² And it happened at that time that Abimelech, and Ochozath his master of ceremonies <note>original: νυμφαγωγὸς (nymphagogos) — literally "one who leads the bride," a high-ranking court official or advisor</note>, and Phicol the commander-in-chief of his army spoke to Abraham, saying, "God is with you in all that you do. ²³ Now therefore, swear to me by God that you will not wrong me, nor my offspring, nor my name; but according to the righteousness <note>or "kindness"</note> that I have shown to you, you shall do to me and to the land in which you have settled." ²⁴ And Abraham said, "I will swear." ²⁵ Then Abraham reproved Abimelech concerning the wells of water which the servants of Abimelech had seized. ²⁶ And Abimelech said to him, "I do not know who did this thing; neither did you report it to me, nor did I hear of it until today." ²⁷ And Abraham took sheep and calves and gave them to Abimelech; and both of them made a covenant. ²⁸ And Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the sheep by themselves. ²⁹ And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What are these seven ewe lambs of the sheep which you have set by themselves?" ³⁰ And Abraham said, "You shall receive these seven ewe lambs from me, so that they may be a witness for me that I dug this well." <margin>§ i</margin> ³¹ For this reason he named the name of that place 'Well of the Oath' <note>original: Φρέαρ ὁρκισμοῦ (Phrear horkismou) — the Greek translation of the Hebrew 'Beersheba'</note>, because there they both swore an oath. ³² And they made a covenant at the Well of the Oath. Then Abimelech rose up, along with Ochozath his master of ceremonies and Phicol the commander-in-chief of his army, <margin>§ Δ₂</margin> and they returned to the land of the Philistines. ³³ And Abraham planted a field <note>original: ἄρουραν (arouran) — often interpreted as a grove or a specific type of tree</note> at the Well of the Oath, and there he called upon the name of the Lord, the Eternal God. ³⁴ And Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines for many days.

**10** [Ephron was sitting] in the midst of the sons of Heth. And Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham and spoke in the hearing of the sons of Heth, <note>original: εἰς τὰ ὦτα (eis ta ōta) — literally "into the ears," a common biblical idiom for "in the hearing of"</note> of all who entered the gate of the city, saying: **11** "Stay with me, lord, and hear me. The field and the cave **11** that is in it I give to you; in the presence of my citizens I have given it to you; bury your dead." **12** And **12** Abraham bowed down before the people of the land; **13** and he spoke to Ephron in the hearing of **13** all the people of the land: "Since you are for me, <note>original: Ἐπειδὴ πρὸς ἐμοῦ εἶ — meaning "Since you are favorable toward me" or "since you are dealing with me"</note> hear me: take the silver for the field from me, and I will bury my dead there." **14** But Ephron answered Abraham, saying: **15** "No, lord, **14 15** for I have heard; a land of four hundred didrachms <note>term: didrachm — a Greek coin worth two drachmas, here used to translate the Hebrew "shekel," the standard unit of weight for silver</note> of silver; between me and you, what would this be? But you, bury your dead." **16** And Abraham listened to Ephron; and Abraham **16** weighed out to Ephron the silver which he had spoken in the hearing of the sons of Heth: four hundred didrachms of silver, approved by merchants. <note>original: δοκίμου ἐμπόροις — silver of a purity or standard recognized by traders</note> **17** And the field of Ephron, which was in the double cave, <note>original: διπλῷ σπηλαίῳ (diplō spēlaiō) — the Septuagint's translation of the name "Machpelah," which in Hebrew suggests "doubled"</note> which is opposite **17** Mamre—the field and the cave which was in it, and every tree which was in the field, which is within its borders round about—**18** was established for Abraham as a possession in the presence of the sons of Heth and all who **18** entered the city. **19** After these things, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the double cave **19** <margin>§ S</margin> of the field, which is opposite Mamre; this is Hebron in the land of Canaan. **20** And **20** the field and the cave that was in it were confirmed to Abraham as a possession for a tomb by the sons of Heth.

"I am Abraham's servant. $^{35}$And the Lord has blessed my master greatly, and he has been exalted; and He has given him sheep and calves, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. $^{36}$And Sarah, my master’s wife, bore <margin>§ S</margin> one son to my master after he had grown old; and he has given $^§$him all that he possessed. $^{37}$And my master made me swear an oath, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the <margin>¶ U₄</margin> daughters of the Canaanites, among whom $^¶$ I $^¶$ dwell as a foreigner in their land; $^{38}$but rather you shall go to the house of <margin>¶ Δ₂</margin> my father $^§$ and to my $^§$ tribe, and from there you shall take a wife for my son.' $^{39}$And I said <margin>§ U₄</margin> to my master, 'What if the woman will not go with me?' $^{40}$And he said to me, 'The Lord God, whom I have pleased <margin>§ Δ₂</margin> in His presence, will Himself send His angel with you and will prosper your way; and you shall take a wife for my son from my tribe and from my father’s house. $^{41}$Then you shall be free <margin>¶ S</margin> from my $^¶$ curse; for whenever you come to my tribe and they do not give her to you, you shall be free from <margin>§ S</margin> my $^§$ oath.' $^{42}$And coming today to the spring, I said, 'Lord, the God of my master Abraham, if You are prospering my way, upon which I am now traveling; $^{43}$behold, I stand by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city will come out to draw water, and it shall be that the maiden to whom I say, "Give me a little water to drink from your pitcher," $^{44}$and she says to me, <margin>¶ Δ₂</margin> "You drink, and I will draw water for your camels too," let this be the woman whom $^¶$ the Lord has prepared for His own servant Isaac; and by this I will know that You have shown mercy to my master Abraham.' $^{45}$And it happened before..."

# GENESIS
## XXIV 55

<margin>56</margin> **55** They said, "Let the young woman stay with us about ten days, and after these things she shall depart." **56** But he said to them, "Do not hold me back, since the Lord has made my way prosperous; send me away so that I may go back to my master."
<margin>57 58</margin> **57** And they said, "Let us call the girl and ask her directly <note>literally: 'ask her mouth'</note>." **58** And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" And she said, "I will go."
<margin>59</margin> **59** And they sent away Rebekah their sister and her belongings <note>The Greek term suggests her possessions or retinue</note>, and the servant of Abraham and those with him.
<margin>60</margin> **60** And they blessed Rebekah their sister and said to her, "You are our sister; may you become thousands of myriads <note>a blessing for countless descendants</note>, and may your offspring inherit the cities of their enemies."
<margin>61</margin> **61** Then Rebekah and her maids arose and mounted the camels and went with the man; and the servant, taking Rebekah, departed.
<margin>62</margin> **62** Now Isaac was traveling through the wilderness by the "Well of Vision" <note>original: 'phrear tēs horaseōs' — likely Beer-lahai-roi</note>; for he lived in the land toward the south.
<margin>63</margin> **63** And Isaac went out to meditate <note>The Greek 'adoleschēsai' can mean to meditate, pray, or simply wander in thought</note> in the field toward evening; and looking up with his eyes, he saw camels coming.
<margin>64</margin> **64** And Rebekah, looking up with her eyes, saw Isaac and jumped down from the camel.
<margin>65</margin> **65** And she said to the servant, "Who is that man walking in the field to meet us?" And the servant said, "He is my master." Then she took her veil and covered herself.
<margin>66</margin> **66** And the servant told Isaac all the things he had done.
<margin>67</margin> **67** And Isaac entered into the house of his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted concerning Sarah his mother.

The elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. $^{17}$ Now Leah's eyes were **weak**; but Rachel was **beautiful in form and lovely in appearance**. $^{18}$ And Jacob **loved** Rachel, and he said, "I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter." $^{19}$ Laban said to him, "It is better for me to give her to you than to give her to another man; stay with me." $^{20}$ And Jacob served seven years for Rachel. $^{21}$ Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, so that I may go in to her." $^{22}$ Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a wedding feast. $^{23}$ And it happened in the evening, taking Leah his daughter, he brought her in to Jacob, and Jacob went in to her. $^{24}$ Laban gave Zilpah, his maidservant, to his daughter Leah to be her maidservant. $^{25}$ And it happened in the morning, and look—it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? And why have you <term>deceived<note>original: "parelogisō." This Greek term implies being cheated or bypassed through a deceptive calculation.</note> me?" $^{26}$ Laban said, "It is not the custom in our place to give the younger before the elder. $^{27}$ Complete this one’s <term>bridal week<note>original: "ta hebdoma." <sup>29</sup> And Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant. <sup>30</sup> And Jacob went in to Rachel; and he loved Rachel more than Leah; and he served Laban for another seven <margin>D</margin> <sup>31</sup> years. <sup>31</sup> And when the Lord God saw that Leah was <term>hated<note>original: "miseitai." In this context, it often implies being "loved less" rather than active hatred, reflecting a comparison between the two wives.</note></term>, he opened her womb; but Rachel was barren. <sup>32</sup> And Leah conceived and bore a son to Jacob; and she called his name <sup>33</sup> **Reuben** <note>The name Reuben sounds like the Hebrew for "See, a son" or "He has seen my misery."</note>, saying, "Because the Lord has seen my humiliation; now my husband will love me." <sup>33</sup> And Leah conceived again and bore a second son to Jacob, and she said, "Because the Lord heard that <sup>34</sup> I am hated, he has given me this one also"; and she called his name **Simeon** <note>The name Simeon is related to the Hebrew word for "hearing."</note>. <sup>34</sup> And she <margin>§ D</margin> conceived yet again and bore a son, and said, "At this present time my husband will be with me, for I have <sup>35</sup> borne him three sons"; for this reason his name was called **Levi** <note>The name Levi is associated with the word for "attached" or "joined."</note>. <sup>35</sup> And she conceived yet again and bore a son, and said, "Now this <sup>§</sup>once more I will give thanks to the Lord"; for this reason she called his name **Judah** <note>The name Judah is derived from the word for "praise" or "thanksgiving."</note>. <margin>§ C<sup>m</sup></margin> And she stopped bearing children.

<margin>XXX 1</margin> <sup>1</sup> And when Rachel saw that she bore no children to Jacob, Rachel became jealous of her sister, and <sup>2</sup> she said to Jacob, "Give me children; if not, I shall die." <sup>2</sup> And Jacob became angry with Rachel and <sup>3</sup> said to her, "Am I in the place of God, who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb?" <sup>3</sup> And Rachel said to Jacob, "Behold my servant Bilhah; go in to her, and she shall give birth upon my knees, <sup>4</sup> so that I too may have children through her." <sup>4</sup> And she gave him her servant Bilhah to be his wife.

...Jacob and in the house of the two handmaids, and he did not find them; then he also entered the house of Rachel. <margin>L</margin>
<margin>34</margin> But Rachel had taken the idols and put them into the camel's saddlebags and sat upon them. <margin>35</margin> And she said to her father, "Do not take it heavily, my lord; I cannot rise before you, for the way of women <note>A polite euphemism for menstruation.</note> is upon me." And Laban searched through the whole house, and did not find the idols. <margin>36</margin> Then Jacob became angry and quarreled with Laban; and answering, Jacob said <margin>37</margin> to Laban, "What is my wrongdoing and what is my sin, that you have hotly pursued after me? And since you have searched all the vessels <note>original: "σκεύη" (skeuē); refers to household goods or containers.</note> of my house, what have you found from all the vessels of your house? Set it here before your brothers and my brothers, and let them judge between the two of us. <margin>38</margin> These twenty years I have been with you; your sheep and your goats have not miscarried; <margin>39</margin> I have not eaten the rams of your sheep; I have not brought to you any animal torn by wild beasts—I made it good myself—thefts by day and thefts by night. <margin>40</margin> I was consumed by the heat of the day and the frost of the night, and my sleep departed from my eyes. <margin>41</margin> These twenty years I have been in your house; I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your sheep, and you cheated <note>original: "παρελογίσω" (parelogisō); to miscalculate or defraud.</note> my wages by ten lambs." <margin>D</margin>

<margin>(26)</margin> [And Jacob was left alone, and] a man wrestled with him until morning. ^{25} And when he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the hollow <note>original: "platous" (πλάτους); literally the breadth or flat part, referring to the hip socket.</note> of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh went numb as he wrestled with him.
<margin>(27)</margin> ^{26} And he said to him, "Let me go, for the dawn has risen." But he said, "I will not let you go unless 
<margin>(28)</margin> <margin>(29)</margin> you bless me." ^{27} And he said to him, "What is your name?" and he said, "Jacob." ^{28} And he said to him, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for you have 
<margin>(30)</margin> prevailed with God, and are powerful with men." ^{29} And Jacob asked and said, "Tell me your name." And he said, "Why is it that you ask my name?" and he blessed him there.
<margin>(31)</margin> ^{30} And Jacob called the name of 그 place "Form of God" <note>original: "Eidos Theou" (Εἶδος θεοῦ); this is the Greek translation of the Hebrew name "Peniel" or "Phanuel," meaning "Face of God."</note>; for he said, "I have seen God face 
<margin>(32)</margin> to face, and my life was preserved." ^{31} And the sun rose upon him when he passed the 
<margin>(33)</margin> "Form of God"; and he limped because of his thigh. ^{32} For this reason the sons of Israel do not eat the nerve that went numb, which is on the hollow of the thigh of Jacob, until 
¶ $L$ ¶ $D$ this day; because he touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh, the nerve, and it went numb.
<margin>1 XXXIII</margin> ^{1} And Jacob looked up and saw, and behold, Esau his brother was coming, and with him four hundred men.

The phrase "a man with him" is found in EGLM and others; the *Speculum* <note>A collection of scriptural quotations</note> reads "an angel with Jacob." | "Until morning" is omitted by Chrysostom. | "Until" is replaced by "as far as" in Clement.
**25** "saw" is replaced by "said" in some copies. | "Indeed" is followed by "he says" in manuscript e. | "The hollow... of Jacob" is rendered as "forbidden nerve" in the Ethiopic version. | "The hollow" is written as "the flat part" in gnp. | "The" (first instance) is replaced by "this" in manuscript w. | The phrase "of him... thigh" (second instance) is omitted in G and Novatian. | "The hollow" (second instance) is preceded by "the nerve over" in the Bohairic version. | "Jacob" is preceded by "of him" or "the" in some manuscripts.
**26** "And he said" is "but he said" in one copy and Cyril. | "To him" is omitted in some copies. | "Let go" is "send away" in some Cyril manuscripts, or "release" in Chrysostom. | "Me" is "to me" in one copy. | "The" is omitted in G and others. | "But he said" is "and he said" in E; "And Jacob said" in the Old Latin; "And he said to him" in the Ethiopic. | "Will let you go" is "will release you" in some versions. | "You bless me" is "me you bless" in D, E, G, L, M and others.
**27** "But he said" is "and he said" in the Armenian and Novatian. | "To him" is omitted in several manuscripts. | "What your name" (28) is omitted in copy f. | "Your name" follows "is" in Novatian. | "To you name" in the Old Latin. | "The" (name) is omitted in G and others. | "Is" is omitted in G, L, and others. | "But he said" is "and he said" in one copy; "and he said to him" in the Ethiopic.
**28** "And he said to him" is omitted in manuscript n. | "And he said" is "but he said" in G, L, and many others. | "To him" is omitted in q and t. | "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob" is "no longer shall Jacob be called your name" in G and others; "no longer shall your name be called" in A and the Armenian version. | "Any longer" is omitted in the Ethiopic and others. | "Because you have prevailed" is "prevailed" in Philo. | "God" is preceded by "the" in several manuscripts. | "With men" is "among men" in the Old Latin. | "Powerful" is preceded by "you shall be" in some copies; "powerfully" in one Philo copy; "you are" in Chrysostom and Novatian; "you have become" in the Old Latin.

“...be fruitful and multiply; and nations and assemblies of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come forth from your loins. ¹² And the land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I have given to you; and to your offspring after you I will give this land.” ¹³ And God went up from him from the place where He had spoken with him. ¹⁴ And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where He had spoken with him, a stone pillar; and he poured a drink offering <note>A libation or liquid offering, usually of wine, poured out as a religious act.</note> upon it, and he poured oil upon it. ¹⁵ And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him there, Bethel <note>Bethel translates to "House of God."</note>.

¹⁶ § (21) 16 ¹⁶ And Jacob departed from Bethel and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Gader <note>Also known as Migdal Eder, or "Tower of the Flock."</note>. § L (16) And it happened when he drew near to Chabratha <note>The Greek transliterates the Hebrew *kivrath*, indicating a certain stretch or distance of land.</note> to come into the land of Ephratha, Rachel gave birth and suffered a hard labor. ¹⁷ And it happened while she was in hard labor, the midwife said to her, “Have courage, for this too is a son for you.” ¹⁸ And it happened as she was giving up her soul—for she was dying—she called his name "Son of my Sorrow" <note>original: *Ben-oni*</note>; but his father called him Benjamin <note>Translates to "Son of the Right Hand," a name of strength or favor.</note>. ¹⁹ And Rachel died, and she was buried on the road to Ephratha—this is Bethlehem. ²⁰ And Jacob set up a pillar upon her tomb; this is the pillar of Rachel's tomb until this very day. ¶ (22) 21 ²¹ And it happened when Israel dwelt in 그 land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, the concubine of his father; and Israel heard of it, and it appeared evil in his sight. ²² Now there were—

# XXXV 22 GENESIS

And the sons of Jacob were twelve. ²³ The sons of Leah: Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, 23
Issachar, and Zebulun. ²⁴ And the sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. ²⁵ And the sons of Bilhah, the handmaid 24
of Rachel: Dan and Naphtali. ²⁶ And the sons of Zilpah, the handmaid of Leah: Gad and Asher. These are the sons 26
of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria <note>A region in the ancient Near East, literally "the land between the rivers."</note>. ²⁷ And Jacob came to Isaac 27
his father at Mamre, to the city of the plain; this is Hebron in the land of Canaan, where
<margin>Section L</margin> Abraham and Isaac had dwelled. ²⁸ And the days of Isaac which he lived were one hundred and eighty 28
years. ²⁹ And Isaac, failing in strength, died and was added to his kin <note>original: "his genus" or "his people," a traditional idiom for death and joining ancestors.</note>, an old man and full 29
<margin>Paragraph L</margin> of days; and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. ¶
¹ And these are the generations of Esau; he is Edom <note>Esau's nickname, meaning "Red."</note>. ² And Esau took for himself wives from ¹ XXXVI
<margin>Section Section</margin> the daughters *of the Canaanites*: Adah, daughter of §Elon the Hittite, and Olibama,
<margin>Section L-variant</margin> daughter of Anah, the son of Zibeon the Hivite, ³ and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael, sister of 3
Nebaioth. ⁴ And Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and †Basemath† bore Reuel, 5 and 4-5
Olibama bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; these are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the
land of Canaan. ⁶ And Esau took his wives and his sons and his daughters and all 6

# GENESIS XXXVI 15

It provides a detailed record of his sons and grandsons through his wives Adah, Basemath, and Oholibamah, including the origins of the Amalekites.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the genealogy of Esau's descendants, specifically the tribal chiefs (clans) arising from his sons Eliphaz, Reuel, and his wife Oholibamah. It transitions into the genealogy of Seir the Horite, the original inhabitants of the land before Edom's dominance.</meta>

# XXXVI 15 GENESIS

...Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Sophar, Chief Kenez, 16 Chief Kore, Chief Gotha, Chief Amalek; these are the chiefs <note>original: "ἡγεμόνες," meaning clan leaders or heads of tribes.</note> of Eliphaz in the land of Idumea <note>original: "Ἰδουμαίᾳ," the Greek name for the territory of Edom.</note>; these are the sons of Adah. 17 And these are the sons of Reuel, the son of Esau: Chief Nachoth, Chief Zerah, Chief Moze, Chief Some; these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath <note>original: "Μασεμμὰθ," a variant of the name Basemath.</note>, the wife of Esau. 18 And these are the sons of Oholibamah, the wife of Esau: Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, Chief Korah; these are the chiefs of Oholibamah. 19 And these are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs; these are their chiefs, the sons of Edom. 20 And these are the sons of Seir the Horite <note>The Horites were the pre-Edomite inhabitants of the region.</note>, who inhabited the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, 21 and Dishon and Ezer and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horite, the son of Seir, in the land of Edom. 22 And the sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and the sister of Lotan was Timna. 23 And these are the sons of Shobal: Alvan and Manahath...

**Textual Notes and Variations**

17 brothers—them] Codex A originally omitted "and he found them" (later corrected in the margin).
18 they saw] spelled differently in manuscripts D and E. | him 1st] manuscript E reads "to him." 22 shed] spelled differently in Codex A. | rescue] spelled differently in Codex D. 23 tunic] spelled differently in Codex E.
25 they sat] spelled differently in Codex A. | Ishmaelites] spelled differently in Codex D and E. 26 brothers] spelled differently in the original hand of manuscript E.

->Manuscript Groups: DE(L)a-yc₂ABELS<-

Latin version (𝔏) | [let us go] "let us depart" in manuscript m; "we shall go" in the Syriac (𝔖). | Dothan 1st] various spellings: Dothaim, Dothaem, Dothain (Philo and Latin). | Omit "and 1st—Dothan 2nd" in manuscript E.

18 This entire verse is omitted in manuscript d. | "Having seen him" in manuscripts f, y, B. | "but"] "for" in manuscript p. | "him 1st"] + "his brothers" in Codex A and B. | "from a distance"] + "from" in manuscript a. | "to kill him"] The majority of manuscripts (D, E, L, etc.) use a word meaning "they acted wickedly" or "plotted wickedly," while a few (A, q, u, y) specifically say "to kill."

19 "they said"] singular "he said" in several manuscripts (a, b, c, etc.). | "his brother"] "his neighbor" in some versions. | "dreamer"] "the dream-seer" in some versions. | "that one"] omitted in manuscript m.

20 Omit "Now therefore" in some versions. | "let us kill"] "we should kill" in manuscripts b, o. | "throw"] slight spelling variations in A, D, E. | "one of the pits"] "the pit" in some versions; + "of these" in others. | "we shall say"] "let us say" in some versions. | "what becomes"] "what will be" in the majority of manuscripts.

21 Reuben] various spellings: Roubin, Roubim, Roubeim. | "from their hands"] "from his hand" in manuscript 107. | "let us not strike"] "do not strike" in the Latin version.

22 "Reuben said to them"] omitted in manuscript d. | "blood"] + "of his" in some Latin versions. | "cast him"] "but cast him" in manuscript 128. | "one of the pits"] "this pit" or "a certain cistern." | "rescue"] "he desired to rescue" in some versions. | "his father"] "their father" in some manuscripts.

23 "to Joseph"] "to him" in some versions. | "the tunic of many colors"] "the varied tunic" or "the colorful robe." | "his tunic"] + "of him" in many manuscripts (A, c, f, etc.).

24 "they threw him"] order reversed in some versions. | "that pit"] + "was empty" in the majority of manuscripts (D, E, etc.). | "no water"] "was empty of water."

25 "to eat bread"] + "of him" (his bread) in some versions. | "looking up"] "and they saw" in some manuscripts. | "Ishmaelites"] + "merchants" in some versions. | "from Gilead"] + "from the land of" in some versions. | "resin and myrrh"] the Greek terms *ritine* and *stakte* refer to valuable aromatic plant resins used for medicine and embalming.

26 "profit"] "gain" or "advantage" (Greek: *chresimon*). | "kill"] some manuscripts use a word meaning "to hide" or "conceal."

18 they conspired] The Greek translators Aquila and Symmachus use a word meaning "they acted deceitfully."
25 incense] Aquila and Symmachus use the term "storax" (a specific resin).

**Ancient Version Notes:**
**6** *troubled*] Aquila: "shaken up"; Symmachus: "gloomy"
**7** *under the*] Aquila and Symmachus: "in the house of the" | *gloomy*] Aquila: "evil"; Symmachus: "wicked/poor"

<summary>Joseph tests his brothers by accusing them of being spies and imprisoning them, eventually demanding they bring their youngest brother to Egypt to prove their honesty. The brothers express deep remorse for their past mistreatment of Joseph, unaware that he understands their speech.</summary>

<margin>XLII 24</margin>

And he returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes. 25 Then Joseph gave orders to fill their containers with grain, and to return the <margin>25</margin> <margin>¶ L</margin> silver of each man ¶ into his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. And it was done <margin>§ L</margin> for them in this way. 26 And after they had placed the grain upon their donkeys, they departed from there. 27 But when one <margin>26 27</margin> opened his sack to give fodder to his donkeys where they stayed for the night, he saw his bundle of silver, and it was at the mouth of the sack. 28 And he said to his brothers, <margin>28</margin> <margin>§ F § D</margin> "My silver has been returned to me, and look, it is here in my sack!" And their hearts failed them, and they were troubled, saying to one another, "What is this that God has done to us?" 29 And they came to Jacob <margin>29</margin> their father in the land of Canaan, and they reported to him all the things that had happened to them, saying, 30 "The man, the lord of the land, spoke harshly to us and put us in custody as though <margin>30</margin> <margin>¶ E § a₂</margin> spying on the land. 31 But we said to him, 'We are men of peace <note>original: εἰρηνικοί (eirēnikoi); often translated as "honest men" in this context</note>, we are not spies; 32 we are twelve <margin>31 32</margin> brothers, sons of our father; one is no more, and the youngest is with our father today in the land of Canaan.' 33 And the man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I shall know that <margin>33</margin> you are men of peace: leave one brother here with me, and take the grain you have purchased for your households and depart; 34 and bring your youngest brother to me, and I shall know that you are not <margin>34</margin> [spies]..."

# GENESIS

### CHAPTER XLIII

<margin>A</margin> **31** ...for his brother, and he sought a place to weep; and having entered into his inner chamber, he wept there. <note>original: ταμιεῖον (tamieion); a private room or storehouse, often used in the Bible to denote a place of seclusion.</note> **31*** And having washed his face, he came out and restrained himself, <margin>d2</margin> and he said, "Serve the bread." **32** And they served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who were dining with him by themselves; for the Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians. <note>Ancient Egyptians historically held a cultural or religious prejudice against nomadic herders, though here it serves to emphasize the separation between the brothers and their hosts.</note> **33** And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his seniority and the younger according to his youth; and the men were astonished, each looking at his brother. **34** And they took portions from him to themselves; and Benjamin’s portion was enlarged five times more than the portions of the others. And they drank and were merry <note>original: ἐμεθύσθησαν (emethysthēsan); while this can mean "became drunk," in a banquet context it often implies drinking freely or being well-satisfied.</note> with him.

### CHAPTER XLIV

<margin>XLIV</margin> **1** And Joseph commanded the one who was over his house, saying, "Fill the men’s sacks with as much food as they are able to carry, and put each man’s silver in the mouth of his sack; **2** and my silver <term>cup|original: κόνδυ (kondy); a specific type of Persian drinking vessel, often associated with divination or high status</term> put into the sack of the youngest, along with the price of his grain." And it was done according to the word that Joseph spoke. **3** When the morning dawned, the men were sent away, they <margin>§</margin> and their donkeys. <margin>§ k</margin> **4** When they had gone out of the city and were not far off, Joseph said to the one over his house, "Arise, pursue after the men, and you shall overtake them and say to them: 'Why have you repaid me evil for good?'"

**4** ...“Why have you returned evil for good? Why have you stolen my silver cup? **5** Is this not the one in which my lord drinks? He himself surely uses it for <term>divination|original: οἰωνισμῷ οἰωνίζεται (oiōnismō oiōnizetai); a practice of seeking omens or hidden knowledge, often involving liquids in a cup</term> in it; you have done evil in what you have accomplished.” **6** And having found them, he spoke these words to them. **7** And they said to him, “Why does my lord speak according to these words?
