...he gave double robes, and to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of gold and five sets of changing robes. ^23 And to his father he sent gifts according to these same things: ten donkeys carrying from all the good things of Egypt, ^24 and ten mules carrying bread for his father for the journey. ^24 Then he sent away his brothers and they departed; and he said to them, "Do not be angry <note>original: ὀργίζεσθε (orgizesthe); meaning 'do not quarrel' or 'do not be agitated'</note> on the way." ^25 And they went up out of Egypt and came into the land of Canaan to Jacob their father, ^26 and they announced it to him, saying, "Your son Joseph is alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt!" And Jacob’s mind was stunned <note>original: ἐξέστη (exestē); literally 'stood outside itself,' indicating shock or disbelief</note>, for he did not believe them. ^27 But they spoke to him all the words spoken by Joseph, as many as he had said to them. And seeing the wagons which Joseph had sent to pick him up, the spirit of Jacob their father revived. ^28 And Israel said, "It is a great thing for me if my son Joseph is still alive; I will go and see him before I die."

<margin>28</margin> 28 And he sent Judah ahead of them to Joseph, to meet him at the City of Heroes <note>original: Ἡρώων πόλιν (Heroon polis); a Greek name for a city in the eastern Nile Delta, likely Pithom.</note> in the land of Rameses. <margin>29</margin> 29 And Joseph, having yoked his chariots, went up to meet Israel his father at the City of Heroes; and appearing to him, he fell upon his neck and wept with a great weeping <note>original: κλαυθμῷ πίονι (klauthmo pioni), literally "a fat/rich weeping," meaning a deep or abundant shedding of tears.</note>. <margin>30</margin> 30 And Israel said to Joseph, "I will die from now on, since I have seen your face; for you are still alive." <margin>31</margin> 31 And Joseph said to his brothers, "Going up, I will report to Pharaoh and I will say to him: 'My brothers and the house of my father, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me; <margin>32</margin> 32 and the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock; and their livestock and oxen and all that is theirs, they have brought.' <margin>33</margin> 33 If, therefore, Pharaoh calls you and says to you, 'What is your occupation?' <margin>34</margin> 34 you shall say, 'We your servants are keepers of livestock from childhood until now, both we and our fathers,' so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen in Arabia <note>The Greek text specifies "Goshen of Arabia," referring to the Arabian Nome or district in Egypt.</note>; for every shepherd of sheep is an abomination <note>original: βδέλυγμα (bdelygma); a thing of ritual or social loathing.</note> to the Egyptians."

<note>The following section represents the 'Apparatus Criticus,' a scholarly list of differences found in various ancient manuscripts of this text. The letters (A, B, D, F, M, etc.) represent specific historical manuscripts.</note>

**A(uid)** | *is left*: Manuscripts A, a, e, g, i, j, s, y and Origen (Greek) read "is left behind"; Codex B and others read "remains" | *before the lord*: one manuscript reads "before you"; others read "our Lord" | *except*: Codex b adds "nothing"; Origen and Chrysostom omit. | *our (3rd)*: one manuscript reads "to us".

**19** *that we might not die*: some manuscripts add "therefore." | *and the land (1st)*: several manuscripts add "even we ourselves." | *be desolate*: some manuscripts use a future tense "will be desolated." | *buy—Pharaoh*: moved to the end of the sentence in one version. | *for bread*: plural "breads" in Codex F and b. | *we shall be*: variant spelling "may we be." | *we*: some manuscripts add "and." | *Pharaoh*: some manuscripts add "the." | *give*: some manuscripts add "to us." | *seeds*: plural in several manuscripts. | *so that we may sow*: omitted in Codex F; several manuscripts add "and we may live." | *the land (3rd)*: one manuscript adds "our." | *will be desolate*: most manuscripts add "not," reading "will NOT be desolate."

**20** *Joseph*: some manuscripts add "the." | *all*: omitted by Chrysostom. | *the land (1st)*: moved after "Egyptians" in one version. | *to Pharaoh (2nd)*: omitted in one Ethiopic version. | *the Egyptians*: one manuscript adds "men." | *their (1st)*: one manuscript reads "to him." | *famine*: one manuscript reads "plague" (a common scribal error in Greek). | *the land (3rd)*: one version reads "their land." | *Pharaoh (3rd)*: several manuscripts add "to the."

**21, 22** The Ethiopic version translates these verses freely.
**21** *enslaved*: one manuscript uses a variant meaning "made them registered." | *to him*: some manuscripts read "to himself." | *as servants*: one manuscript reads "to the end." | *from the ends of the borders*: one version reads "from the beginning of the end." | *borders*: variant spellings "mountains" or "seasons." | *to the ends (2nd)*: some manuscripts add "of them" or "of it."

**22** *except*: moved after "land" in some versions. | *only*: various plural/singular grammatical forms in different manuscripts. | *did not buy this*: some manuscripts omit "this"; others add "for Pharaoh." | *gave (1st)*: some read "has given." | *grant*: plural "grants" in several manuscripts. | *priests (1st)*: one manuscript adds "then." | *Pharaoh (1st)*: one manuscript adds "from." | *and—Pharaoh (2nd)*: marked as a doubtful passage in Codex M. | *ate—was*: one version reads "ate that which." | *Pharaoh (2nd)*: one manuscript reads "Joseph." | *for this reason*: one manuscript adds "for."

**23** *to all*: moved after "Egyptians" in one manuscript; omitted in others. | *I have bought*: one manuscript reads "he has bought." | *us*: variant "you." | *and (1st)—your*: moved after "today" in several manuscripts. | *seed*: plural "seeds" in many manuscripts. | *the land (2nd)*: one manuscript reads "it."

**24** *it shall be—of its*: several manuscripts add "if/when it is produced." | *produce*: variant spelling "offspring." | *its*: one manuscript reads "the land's." | *you shall give*: some manuscripts add "and." | *the (1st)*: omitted in one manuscript. | *for yourselves (1st)*: one manuscript reads "and it." | *for seed*: plural "for seeds" in some manuscripts. | *the land*: one manuscript adds "in." | *for you (2nd)*: variant "for us" or "of you." | *and for food*: Codex M adds "and for food for your infants." | *households*: some manuscripts use the word "houses." | *your (2nd)*: several manuscripts add "and for food for your infants."

**25** *they said*: variant spelling. | *saved*: one version translates this as "healed." | *we have found*: various past tense forms "we found," "we have found," or "we might find." | *before our lord*: one version reads "before you, lord." | *we shall be*: variant spelling. | *servants of Pharaoh*: one manuscript reads "his domestics." | *Pharaoh*: some manuscripts add "to the."

**26** *and*: Chrysostom reads "and this." | *them*: variant "him." | *Joseph*: moved after "ordinance." | *as an ordinance*: (text cuts off).

---

<note>Scholarly marginalia translated:</note>
**19** *buy*: Codex F clarifies "purchase."
**21** *registered them*: Codex c₂ explains "enslaved" as "made them registered subjects."
**22** *because—priests*: Aquila's translation: "because it was a precise portion for the priests." Symmachus's translation: "for there was a set allowance for the priests." Samaritan version: "for there was a portion for the priests."

<summary>This page contains the Septuagint Greek text and extensive scholarly notes for Genesis 48:12-18, where Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. The passage is famous for Jacob intentionally crossing his hands to give the younger son the primary blessing, an act that Joseph unsuccessfully tries to correct.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the deathbed scene of Jacob (Israel). Having crossed his hands to favor Joseph's younger son Ephraim, Jacob now explains his reasoning and delivers his final prophetic blessings to his sons, beginning with his firstborn, Reuben. This transcription includes a complex critical apparatus—the small-print notes at the bottom used by scholars to track differences between ancient manuscript versions like the Septuagint, the Latin Vulgate, and the Samaritan Pentateuch.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the prophetic blessings of the patriarch Jacob as he lies on his deathbed. Having rebuked his firstborn, Reuben, for his instability and past transgressions, Jacob now turns his attention to his next sons—Simeon, Levi, and Judah. The text is presented with a complex scholarly apparatus at the bottom, which lists variations found in different ancient manuscripts, such as the Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Alexandrinus (A), and various early translations like the Latin (L) and Sahidic Coptic (S).</meta>

### Critical Apparatus

**10** **A ruler from Judah:** written over an erasure in manuscript A¹. | **from Judah:** "in Judah" according to Irenaeus. | **and [1°]:** "nor" in several manuscripts and early versions including Justin Martyr, Hippolytus, Origen, and Eusebius. | **from—his:** "out of Israel" according to Origen. | **him:** "you" in Theodoret. | **until [αν]:** omitted in some versions of Chrysostom and Theodoret. | **come [ελθοι]:** variant in manuscripts g and i. | **the things laid up for him:** "their things laid up" in a₂; "the thing laid up for him which is laid up" in m; "he for whom the things are laid up" in Origen; "he for whom they are prepared" in the Armenian; "to whom they were stored" in the Latin Origen; "the one for whom it is laid up" in several manuscripts (c₂, d, f, g, etc.), Justin Martyr, Eusebius, and Chrysostom. | **he:** "this is" in Chrysostom; "it is he" in Hilary; adds "shall be" in Justin, Hippolytus, and others; adds "is" in the Armenian and Irenaeus. | **nations:** adds "is" in manuscript l.

**11** **the foal [1°]:** "the donkey" in Hippolytus and Theodoret. | **and [1°]—his [2°]:** omitted by Justin Martyr. | **to the branch:** adds "in" in Hippolytus; "to the hair-cloth" in the Latin; "to the manger" in the Old Latin; adds "of the vine" in Theodoret. | **the foal [2°]—donkey:** "the beast of burden" in Eusebius. | **his [2°]:** omitted in several manuscripts and by Justin and Irenaeus. | **shall wash:** variant spelling in a₂. | **in wine [1°]—him [4°]:** "in the blood of the grape his robe" in Justin. | **in wine:** placed after "him" in Novatian. | **his [3°]:** adds "his eyes are joyful" in m*. | **the garment:** "the cloak" or "outer garment" in some manuscripts and the Latin.

**12** **joyful:** "fearful" in Cyprian; "shining" in the Latin. | **beyond wine:** "from wine" in most manuscripts (A, D, F, M) and Fathers; "as wine" in Chrysostom. | **white:** omitted in manuscript l. | **his [2°]:** omitted in D and F*. | **than milk:** "from milk" in some Latin translations. | **than [η]:** "as" in Armenian, Coptic, and Latin versions. | **milk:** "of milk" in Hippolytus.

**13** **Zebulun:** variant spelling in c and s. | **coast:** adds "of the seas" in several manuscripts and the Armenian. | **shall dwell:** variant in D. | **by a harbor of ships:** "shall be a protection of ships" in the Latin. | **harbor:** variant spelling in c, d, i, m, n. | **ships:** singular "ship" in f* and Cyril. | **extend:** variant spellings in v and b₂. | **Sidon:** variant spelling in B and i; "Sydonia" in the Old Latin.

**14** **Issachar:** variant spellings in F, d, e, f, l, m, etc. | **that which is good:** "an ox" in the Latin. | **resting:** omitted in m. | **in the midst:** variant preposition in A, d, n, y.

**15** **the rest:** omitted in f. | **that it was good:** "which is good" in the Latin. | **the land:** repeated in manuscript c. | **rich:** variant spelling in c. | **subjected:** variant spelling in k. | **his:** omitted by Philo and Origen. | **labor:** "to do" in some manuscripts. | **became:** variant spellings in f, g, k, l, b, n, s, Philo, and Chrysostom. | **husbandman:** adds "of the earth" in some manuscripts.

---

**10** **the things laid up for him:** "he for whom it is laid up" in F; "he for whom it is, which is..." in M. | **and [2°]—nations:** Aquila: "and to him a gathering of peoples."
**11** **and to the branch:** "and to the vine-shoot" in F.
**12** **joyful:** Aquila: "dark" or "saturated"; others say "saturated, hot, fiery, terrible."
**13** **extend:** Aquila: "his thigh [side]."
**14** **desired that which is good:** "a bony donkey" in F; Aquila: "a bony donkey." | **of the allotments:** "of the meadows" in F.
**15** **and [3°]—husbandman:** Samaritikon: "and he is a farmer to serve." | **a husbandman:** Aquila: "serving for tribute"; others say "serving tribute." | **man:** "human" in manuscript ν.

### CHAPTER 49, VERSES 16–23

<margin>16</margin>
->$^{16}$ Dan shall judge his own people,<-
->as also one tribe in Israel.<-
<margin>17</margin>
->$^{17}$ And let Dan become a serpent on the road,<-
->sitting upon the path,<-
->biting the horse’s heel,<-
->and the rider shall fall backward,<-
<margin>18</margin>
->$^{18}$ waiting for the salvation of the Lord. <note>original: τὴν σωτηρίαν περιμένων Κυρίου (tēn sōtērian perimenōn Kyriou); This is a famous liturgical exclamation where Jacob pauses his blessing to express his hope in God's deliverance.</note><-
<margin>19</margin>
->$^{19}$ Gad, a troop of raiders shall raid him;<-
->but he shall raid them at their heels. <note>original: πειρατήριον πειρατεύσει (peiratērion peirateusei); The Greek preserves the wordplay found in the Hebrew text, where the name Gad sounds like the words for "troop" and "raid."</note><-
<margin>20</margin>
->$^{20}$ Asher, his bread is rich,<-
->and he shall provide luxuries for rulers.<-
<margin>21</margin>
->$^{21}$ Naphtali is a spreading stem,<-
->yielding beauty in its fruit. <note>original: στέλεχος ἀνειμένον (stelechos aneimenon); The Greek translators understood this as a botanical metaphor ("spreading stem/trunk"), whereas the Hebrew text describes Naphtali as a "doe set free."</note><-
<margin>22</margin>
->$^{22}$ Joseph is an increased son,<-
->my increased son, one to be envied;<-
->my youngest son;<-
->return to me. <note>original: πρὸς μὲ ἀνάστρεψον (pros me anastrepson); The Greek translation of this verse is quite different from the Hebrew, which speaks of a "fruitful bough by a spring." Here, it takes on a more personal, emotive tone from father to son.</note><-
<margin>23</margin>
->$^{23}$ Against whom those taking counsel reviled him,<-
->and the lords of the arrows held a grudge against him;<-

### GENESIS 49:24–29

<margin>24</margin>
$^{24}$ And their bows were shattered with might,
and the sinews of their arms were loosened,
by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob; <note>original: δυνάστου Ἰακώβ (dynastou Iakōb); This title refers to God as the "Powerful One" or "Potentate" of the patriarch Jacob.</note>
from there is the one who strengthened Israel;
<margin>(25)</margin> by the God of your father.
<margin>25</margin>
$^{25}$ And my God helped you,
and he blessed you with a blessing of heaven from above,
and a blessing of the earth containing all things; <note>The Greek text emphasizes the "fullness" of the earth's blessing, whereas the Hebrew tradition often focuses on "the deep that lies below."</note>
for the sake of the blessings of the breasts and of the womb,
<margin>26</margin>
$^{26}$ the blessings of your father and your mother;
it has prevailed over the blessings of the permanent mountains,
and over the blessings of the everlasting hills; <note>original: θινῶν ἀενάων (thinōn aenaōn); Literally "everlasting heaps" or "dunes," usually interpreted as the ancient hills.</note>
they shall be upon the head of Joseph,
and upon the crown of the head of the brothers whom he led. <note>original: ὧν ἡγήσατο (hōn hēgēsato); This refers to Joseph as the leader or "prince" among his brothers during their time in Egypt.</note>
<margin>27</margin>
$^{27}$ Benjamin is a ravening wolf;
in the morning he still eats,
and toward the evening he gives food. <note>In the Greek tradition, Benjamin is depicted as a successful hunter who provides for others, whereas the Hebrew text says he "divides the spoil."</note>

->THE TEXT OF THE <term>SEPTUAGINT</term> <note>original: "Septuaginta"; The oldest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which legend says was translated by seventy-two Jewish scholars.</note><-

# THE OLD TESTAMENT
## IN GREEK

->ACCORDING TO THE TEXT OF <term>CODEX VATICANUS</term> <note>One of the oldest and most important surviving Greek manuscripts of the Bible, dating to the 4th century AD; it is named for its home in the Vatican Library.</note>, SUPPLEMENTED FROM OTHER <term>UNCIAL</term> <note>A formal style of ancient handwriting using large, rounded capital letters, commonly used for prestigious manuscripts between the 3rd and 8th centuries.</note> MANUSCRIPTS, WITH A <term>CRITICAL APPARATUS</term> <note>A scholarly system of footnotes that documents every variation found in other ancient copies, allowing researchers to compare sources and determine the most original text.</note> CONTAINING THE VARIANTS OF THE CHIEF ANCIENT AUTHORITIES FOR THE TEXT OF THE <term>SEPTUAGINT</term> <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to have been translated by seventy scholars. It was the version of the scriptures most commonly used by the early Christian Church.</note><-

->WITH A <term>CRITICAL APPARATUS</term> <note>A detailed set of notes at the bottom of a page that lists every variation or "typo" found in other ancient versions of the text, allowing scholars to see how the wording changed over time.</note> CONTAINING THE<-

# THE OLD TESTAMENT IN GREEK

## ACCORDING TO THE TEXT OF <term>CODEX VATICANUS</term> <note>One of the oldest and most important surviving Greek manuscripts of the Bible, dating to the 4th century AD. It has been housed in the Vatican Library since at least the 15th century.</note>, SUPPLEMENTED FROM OTHER <term>UNCIAL</term> <note>A formal style of ancient handwriting consisting of large, rounded capital letters, used primarily in prestigious books like Bibles from the 3rd to 8th centuries.</note> MANUSCRIPTS, WITH A <term>CRITICAL APPARATUS</term> <note>A detailed set of notes at the bottom of a page that lists every variation or difference found in other ancient versions of the text, allowing scholars to see how the wording changed across different manuscripts.</note> CONTAINING THE VARIANTS OF THE CHIEF ANCIENT AUTHORITIES FOR THE TEXT OF THE <term>SEPTUAGINT</term> <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to have been translated by seventy Jewish scholars in Alexandria. It was the version most frequently used by early Christians.</note>

->EDITED BY<-

<margin>
BS
41
.B7
v. 1
pt. 1
</margin>

->ALAN ENGLAND BROOKE, <term>B.D.</term> <note>Bachelor of Divinity, a senior academic degree in theology.</note><-
->FELLOW AND DEAN OF KING’S COLLEGE,<-
->AND<-
->NORMAN McLEAN, <term>M.A.</term> <note>Master of Arts.</note><-
->FELLOW OF CHRIST’S COLLEGE, UNIVERSITY LECTURER IN <term>ARAMAIC</term> <note>A Semitic language closely related to Hebrew, which was the common language of the Near East and parts of the Bible.</note>.<-

->Cambridge University Press<-
->London: Bentley House, 200 Euston Road, N.W.1<-
->1906<-

It establishes the text based on the famous 4th-century Codex Vaticanus and provides a comprehensive system for comparing it to other ancient sources.</summary>
